title: Changing parameters after an oral dose

segs.text: Module five, objective four. What happens after an oral dose when one parameter changes. The question is how C max, t max and A U C change, and the answers are directions: up, down or unchanged. A U C, the area under the plasma concentration time curve, measures the extent of exposure: how much drug got in and how long it stayed. Two relations decide every direction. t max uses only k a and k, and A U C equals F times the dose over clearance, where clearance equals k times V D. k a is in neither A U C line, so A U C depends on the dose, F and the clearance, but not on k a.

card.m: one change → C<sub>max</sub>, t<sub>max</sub>, AUC: up, down or unchanged
AUC: D<sub>0</sub>, F, Cl (k × V<sub>D</sub>); not k<sub>a</sub>

segs.text: Raise the dose, and C max and A U C rise in proportion, while t max stays where it was. More drug means larger amounts absorbed and eliminated per hour, but the rate constants, the fractions per hour, do not change, so the peak comes at the same time. She said, If I increase the dose, what happens to t max? Nothing, right? In her Example one, doubling the dose from five hundred to one thousand milligrams keeps t max at two hours, doubles C max from twelve point one seven to twenty four point three four milligrams per liter, and doubles A U C.

card.m: dose up: C<sub>max</sub> and AUC up in proportion, t<sub>max</sub> unchanged
rates (mg/hr) up; k and k<sub>a</sub> (hr<sup>−1</sup>) unchanged

segs.text: Raise k a with k unchanged, and the drug gets in faster, so C max is higher and t max earlier. A U C stays about the same, because k a is not part of the clearance. In the textbook table, with k at zero point one per hour, raising k a from zero point two to zero point six per hour moves t max from six point nine three to three point five eight hours and raises C max from five to six point nine nine micrograms per milliliter, while A U C stays at one hundred. She said, looking at the curve, you might not be able to really ascertain, but this comes from your textbook, and this is tabulated, and the A U C is relatively unchanged.

card.m: k<sub>a</sub> up, k fixed: C<sub>max</sub> up, t<sub>max</sub> earlier
AUC for a k<sub>a</sub> change: from the table, not the curves

segs.text: Raise k with k a unchanged, and the drug leaves faster, so C max is lower, t max is earlier, and A U C falls. A U C falls because clearance equals k times V D, so a larger k is a larger clearance. She said, if we change the K, we are effectively changing the clearance. The trap is to expect a later peak with faster elimination, but t max falls when either constant rises. Swapping the two constants gives the same t max but a different A U C, because k has changed.

card.m: k up, k<sub>a</sub> fixed: C<sub>max</sub> down, t<sub>max</sub> earlier, AUC down
Cl = k × V<sub>D</sub> up → AUC down
e.g. (Ch 16 Table 16-2, k<sub>a</sub> 0.3 hr<sup>−1</sup>) k 0.1 → 0.5 hr<sup>−1</sup>: t<sub>max</sub> 5.49 → 2.55 hr, C<sub>max</sub> 5.77 → 2.79 mcg/mL, AUC 100 → 20 mcg·hr/mL
k<sub>a</sub> 0.1, k 0.2 vs k<sub>a</sub> 0.2, k 0.1 hr<sup>−1</sup>: t<sub>max</sub> 6.93 hr both; AUC 50 vs 100 mcg·hr/mL

segs.text: Two terms say which process is slower. Disposition rate limiting, the usual case, means the absorption half-life is much shorter than the elimination half-life, so k a is much larger than k. Absorption rate limiting means the absorption half-life is much longer than the elimination half-life. She once said distribution limited for the usual case, but the term to use is disposition rate limiting. The textbook notes that in an extended release product absorption is slower than elimination, so the last, falling part of the curve shows absorption, not elimination, which is called flip flop, and the true k then needs I V data.

card.m: disposition rate limiting: t½<sub>a</sub> ≪ t½, k<sub>a</sub> ≫ k (usual)
flip-flop: the falling part shows k<sub>a</sub>; true k from IV data

segs.text: Her slide Example two asks which case an antibiotic is. Its exponents give k a, two point seven five, and k, zero point two two per hour. The absorption half-life is zero point two five two hours and the elimination half-life three point one five hours, so absorption is twelve point five times faster. The drug is disposition rate limiting, the usual case. A question may give two exponents to compare directly: with e to the minus zero point one eight against e to the minus zero point eight seven, absorption is much faster than elimination.

card.m: t½<sub>a</sub> = {{frac:0.693|2.75 hr<sup>−1</sup>}} = 0.252 hr   t½ = {{frac:0.693|0.22 hr<sup>−1</sup>}} = 3.15 hr

segs.text: Her exam review asked what to expect with a two-fold increase in oral dose, select all that apply, and by her rule the answers are increased A U C and increased C max; both t max options are wrong. Her attendance poll asked what results when an oral dose is increased, and she was looking for no change in t max. k a, t max and C max matter for designing multiple dose regimens, for bioequivalence, for choosing the route and dosage form, for the onset of action, and for relating concentration to effect.

card.m: poll: dose up → no change in tmax
uses: regimens, bioequivalence, route and form, onset, effect
